374:     const op = batch.opcodes[i]!;
375:     try {
376:       switch (op.category) {
377:         case CAT_TREE:
378:           applyTree(op, renderer, touchedFitGates);
379:           break;
380:         case CAT_PARAMETER:
381:           applyStyle(op, batch.strings, renderer);
382:           break;
383:         case CAT_META:
384:           applyMeta(op, batch.strings, renderer);
385:           break;
386:         default:
387:           break;
388:       }
389:     } catch (err) {
390:       // The batch is a renderer-consuming instruction stream; an empty catch
391:       // would hide a structural bug. Log the exact op for remote diagnosis,
392:       // then rethrow (the host's handleMessage surfaces it).
393:       const el = renderer.byId.get(op.a);
394:       const where = el instanceof Element
395:         ? `${el.tagName.toLowerCase()}#${el.getAttribute("data-pathland-id")}.${el.className}`
396:         : String(el);
397:       console.error(
398:         `[pathland] applyBatch failed at op ${i}/${batch.opcodes.length} ` +
399:         `cat=${op.category} cmd=${op.command} a=${op.a} b=${op.b} c=${op.c} target=${where}`, err);
400:       throw err;
401:     }
402:   }
403:   for (const slot of touchedFitGates) {
404:     reconcileFitGate(slot);
405:   }
406:   // Derived layout (fill propagation, ZStack sizing/positioning, cross-axis
407:   // align-self) — mirrors the Rust SSR renderer's whole-tree decisions.
408:   applyLayout(renderer);
409: }

411: function applyMeta(op: Opcode, strings: Uint8Array, r: DomRenderer): void {
412:   switch (op.command) {
413:     case CMD_RESET: {
414:       for (const el of Array.from(r.byId.values())) {
415:         if (el.parentNode) {
416:           el.parentNode.removeChild(el);
417:         }
418:       }
419:       r.byId.clear();
420:       break;
421:     }
422:     case CMD_SET_COLOR_SCHEME: {
423:       const root = document.documentElement;
424:       if (op.a === COLOR_SCHEME_LIGHT) {
425:         root.dataset.pathlandScheme = "light";
426:       } else if (op.a === COLOR_SCHEME_DARK) {
427:         root.dataset.pathlandScheme = "dark";
428:       } else {
429:         delete root.dataset.pathlandScheme;
430:       }
431:       break;
432:     }
433:     case CMD_RESET_THEME:
434:       (r.tokenSink ??= createTokenSink()).reset();
435:       break;
436:     case CMD_SET_WINDOW_METADATA: {
437:       // Renderer-global surface metadata (spec/OPCODE.md §Window metadata). The
438:       // browser mapping: title → document.title, description → meta description,
439:       // locale → <html lang>. An empty value clears the field.
440:       const value = readString(strings, op.b);
441:       switch (op.a) {
442:         case WINDOW_TITLE:
443:           document.title = value || (r.defaultTitle ?? "Pathland");
444:           break;
445:         case WINDOW_DESCRIPTION:
446:           setMetaDescription(value);
447:           break;
448:         case WINDOW_LOCALE:
449:           if (value) {
450:             document.documentElement.lang = value;
451:           } else {
452:             document.documentElement.removeAttribute("lang");
453:           }
454:           break;
455:         default:
456:           break;
457:       }
458:       break;
459:     }
460:     case CMD_ENVIRONMENT:
461:     default:
462:       break;
463:   }
464: }

466: /** Update (or remove, for an empty value) the document's meta description. */
467: function setMetaDescription(value: string): void {
468:   const existing = document.head.querySelector<HTMLMetaElement>('meta[name="description"]');
469:   if (!value) {
470:     existing?.remove();
471:     return;
472:   }
473:   const meta = existing ?? document.createElement("meta");
474:   if (!existing) {
475:     meta.setAttribute("name", "description");
476:     document.head.appendChild(meta);
477:   }
478:   meta.setAttribute("content", value);
479: }

481: /** The node actually inserted into a parent's container: ZStack children are
482:  *  wrapped in a `grid-area:1/1` cell shell, grid cells (a GRID's bare children
483:  *  or a GRID_ROW's children) in an auto-placed cell shell (the layout pass sets
484:  *  their `justify-self`/`align-self` and explicit `grid-row`/`grid-column` from
485:  *  the container's structure/ALIGNMENT — mirrors the Rust SSR renderer), a
486:  *  GRID_ROW itself inserts directly (it is the row container, not a cell);
487:  *  everything else inserts directly. */
488: function placedChild(parent: Node, child: Node): Node {
489:   if (child instanceof HTMLElement) {
490:     const parentComp = componentByNode.get(parent);
491:     if (parentComp === COMPONENT_ZSTACK) {
492:       const wrapper = document.createElement("div");
493:       wrapper.style.gridArea = "1/1";
494:       wrapper.appendChild(child);
495:       return wrapper;
496:     }
497:     if (isGridComponent(parentComp) || parentComp === COMPONENT_GRID_ROW) {
498:       if (componentByNode.get(child) === COMPONENT_GRID_ROW) {
499:         return child; // a row container is a grid child, not a cell
500:       }
501:       const wrapper = document.createElement("div");
502:       wrapper.appendChild(child);
503:       return wrapper;
504:     }
505:   }
506:   return child;
507: }

509: /** Materialize a PICKER's child TEXT node as a native `<option>` (the Rust SSR
510:  *  renderer emits `<option data-pathland-id="{child}" value="{index}">` per
511:  *  child). The option keeps the child's id so its PARAMETER deltas resolve to it. */
512: function pickerOption(child: HTMLElement): HTMLElement {
513:   const opt = document.createElement("option");
514:   opt.textContent = child.textContent ?? "";
515:   const id = child.getAttribute("data-pathland-id");
516:   if (id) {
517:     opt.setAttribute("data-pathland-id", id);
518:   }
519:   return opt;
520: }

522: /** Keep a PICKER's option `value` attributes aligned with their index (the SSR
523:  *  renderer's `<option value="{i}">` scheme). */
524: function renumberPickerOptions(container: Node): void {
525:   if (!(container instanceof HTMLSelectElement)) {
526:     return;
527:   }
528:   Array.from(container.options).forEach((o, i) => {
529:     o.value = String(i);
530:   });
531: }

533: function applyTree(op: Opcode, r: DomRenderer, touchedFitGates: Set<HTMLElement>): void {
534:   // N→1 fit-slot reconcile (issue #141): the server's SSR snapshot carried EVERY
535:   // candidate behind CSS `@container` gated wrappers (`data-pathland-fit-cands`).
536:   // The downgrade to a single selected child is signalled by REMOVING a candidate
537:   // (a `REMOVE_CHILD`/`DELETE_NODE` on the slot). Record the touched slot and
538:   // reconcile it AFTER the batch (`reconcileFitGate`), once the REMOVE/DELETE
539:   // deltas have applied: only a slot that actually ended up with a single live
540:   // candidate is the downgrade — a removal that merely drops a child inside a
541:   // candidate (a band-crossing fit swap) must leave the gate intact. An
542:   // `INSERT_CHILD`/`CREATE_NODE` is never the downgrade: a `META::RESYNC` replays
543:   // the whole tree and the SSR gate must SURVIVE it (the CSS band keeps showing the
544:   // width-correct candidate).
545:   if (op.command === CMD_REMOVE_CHILD || op.command === CMD_DELETE_NODE) {
546:     const slot = nearestGatedFitSlot(op, r);
547:     if (slot) {
548:       touchedFitGates.add(slot);
549:     }
550:   }
551:   switch (op.command) {
552:     case CMD_CREATE_NODE: {
553:       // Hydration-aware: an id already present in the registry is the SSR-hydrated
554:       // element — reuse it (a resync/full snapshot replays CREATE for every node
555:       // without clobbering the visible DOM). Only create a fresh shell when absent.
556:       let el = r.byId.get(op.a);
557:       if (!el) {
558:         el = createElement(op.b);
559:         if (el.nodeType === Node.ELEMENT_NODE) {
560:           (el as HTMLElement).setAttribute("data-pathland-id", String(op.a));
561:         }
562:         r.byId.set(op.a, el);
563:       }
564:       if (el.nodeType === Node.ELEMENT_NODE) {
565:         componentByNode.set(el, op.b);
566:       }
567:       break;
568:     }
569:     case CMD_DELETE_NODE: {
570:       const el = r.byId.get(op.a);
571:       if (el) {
572:         const host = el as HTMLElement;
573:         // `DELETE_NODE` covers the whole subtree: every descendant's registry
574:         // entry must die too, or a later op could reuse a still-registered
575:         // (detached) element and double-parent it (HierarchyRequestError).
576:         purgeSubtreeRegistry(host, r);
577:         if (host.parentNode) {
578:           host.parentNode.removeChild(host);
579:         }
580:       }
581:       r.byId.delete(op.a);
582:       break;
583:     }
584:     case CMD_INSERT_CHILD: {
585:       const child = r.byId.get(op.b);
586:       const parentNode = r.byId.get(op.a);
587:       if (!child || !parentNode) {
588:         break;
589:       }
590:       let parent: Node = parentNode;
591:       // A `VIDEO` surface gaining custom control children morphs its bare
592:       // `<video>` into a `.pathland-media` wrapper (the Rust SSR emits the same
593:       // structure); the children then attach to the wrapper.
594:       const comp = componentByNode.get(parentNode);
595:       if (comp === COMPONENT_VIDEO
596:           && parentNode instanceof HTMLElement && parentNode.matches("video")) {
597:         parent = mediaToWrapper(parentNode, r);
598:       }
599:       const container = childrenContainer(parent);
600:       // Hydration/idempotent-replay guard: skip when the child is already there
601:       // (the SSR DOM already holds the initial tree; a resync replays it), or
602:       // when a duplicate of the node already exists by id (drift protection —
603:       // never render a second copy the app did not emit).
604:       if (container && !container.contains(child)
605:           && !(child instanceof Element && container instanceof Element
606:             && container.querySelector(`[data-pathland-id="${op.b}"]`))) {
607:         let placed = placedChild(parent, child);
608:         if (comp === COMPONENT_PICKER && child instanceof HTMLElement) {
609:           // Picker children are option labels → materialize native `<option>`s.
610:           placed = pickerOption(child);
611:           r.byId.set(op.b, placed);
612:           componentByNode.set(placed, COMPONENT_TEXT);
613:         }
614:         insertAt(container, placed, op.c);
615:         if (comp === COMPONENT_PICKER) {
616:           renumberPickerOptions(container);
617:         }
618:         maybeAnimateInsert(parent, placed);
619:       }
620:       break;
621:     }
622:     case CMD_REMOVE_CHILD: {
623:       const child = r.byId.get(op.b);
624:       if (child && child.parentNode) {
625:         child.parentNode.removeChild(child);
626:       }
627:       break;
628:     }
629:     case CMD_MOVE_CHILD: {
630:       const child = r.byId.get(op.b);
631:       if (!child) {
632:         break;
633:       }
634:       const parent = r.byId.get(op.a);
635:       if (parent) {
636:         const container = childrenContainer(parent);
637:         if (container) {
638:           // Detach the child (and its now-empty ZStack wrapper, if any) so the
639:           // wrapper-count stays in sync with the Rust SSR structure.
640:           const oldParent = child.parentNode;
641:           child.parentNode?.removeChild(child);
642:           if (
643:             oldParent instanceof HTMLElement &&
644:             oldParent !== container &&
645:             oldParent.childElementCount === 0 &&
646:             oldParent.style.position === "absolute"
647:           ) {
648:             oldParent.remove();
649:           }
650:           let placed = placedChild(parent, child);
651:           if (componentByNode.get(parent) === COMPONENT_PICKER && child instanceof HTMLElement) {
652:             placed = pickerOption(child);
653:             r.byId.set(op.b, placed);
654:             componentByNode.set(placed, COMPONENT_TEXT);
655:           }
656:           insertAt(container, placed, op.c);
657:           if (componentByNode.get(parent) === COMPONENT_PICKER) {
658:             renumberPickerOptions(container);
659:           }
660:         }
661:       }
662:       break;
663:     }
664:     default:
665:       break;
666:   }
667: }

669: function insertAt(container: Node, child: Node, index: number): void {
670:   // Inserting a node into itself or its own subtree yields an incorrect node
671:   // tree — the child is effectively already positioned; skip (never throw).
672:   if (child === container || container.contains(child)) {
673:     return;
674:   }
675:   // The protocol's INSERT/MOVE index counts ELEMENT children. Debug-comment
676:   // nodes (`<!-- #id … -->`, `pathland.debug-html=true`) are sibling children
677:   // in the SSR-hydrated DOM, so counting them in `visible` shifts every index
678:   // and e.g. would insert a trailing sidebar BEFORE the main area. Count
679:   // elements only; the injected nav-back button is excluded by class.
680:   const visible = Array.from(container.childNodes).filter(
681:     (n) =>
682:       n.nodeType === Node.ELEMENT_NODE &&
683:       !(n instanceof HTMLElement && n.classList.contains(NAV_BACK_CLASS)),
684:   );
685:   const target = visible[index];
686:   detachIfWrongParent(container, child);
687:   if (target) {
688:     if (target === child || target.contains(child)) {
689:       // Would yield an incorrect node tree (inserting a node before itself or a
690:       // descendant) — the child is already positioned; nothing to do.
691:       return;
692:     }
693:     container.insertBefore(child, target);
694:   } else {
695:     container.appendChild(child);
696:   }
697: }

699: // --- renderer-provided navigation chrome (spec DSL.md §4.5) ---
700: // A `PlatformDefault` nav slot at depth > 1 gets a default back button drawn by
701: // the DOM renderer (the web has no native navigation container). The button is
702: // a tracked child of the slot that the reconcile ignores (see `insertAt`), so
703: // TREE deltas never displace it. `Custom` chrome slots never get one.
704: 
705: /** The injected default back button's class (excluded from child indexing). */
706: export const NAV_BACK_CLASS = "pathland-nav-back";
707: 
708: /** Whether an element is a nav slot (carries a `data-pathland-route`). */
709: function isNavSlot(el: HTMLElement): boolean {
710:   return el.hasAttribute("data-pathland-route");
711: }
712: 
713: /** The slot's chrome mode: `true` when the developer owns all nav UI. */
714: function isCustomChrome(el: HTMLElement): boolean {
715:   return el.getAttribute("data-pathland-nav-chrome") === "custom";
716: }
717: 
718: /** The slot's current depth (defaults to 1 = root destination). */
719: function slotDepth(el: HTMLElement): number {
720:   return Math.max(1, Number(el.getAttribute("data-pathland-depth") ?? "1") || 1);
721: }
722: 
723: /** The injected back button inside a slot, if present. */
724: function injectedBackButton(el: HTMLElement): HTMLButtonElement | null {
725:   return el.querySelector<HTMLButtonElement>(`.${NAV_BACK_CLASS}`);
726: }
727: 
728: /**
729:  * Reconcile the renderer's default back button for a nav slot: shown for a
730:  * `PlatformDefault` slot at depth > 1, removed for `Custom` chrome or depth 1.
731:  * Called from `SET_PROPERTY` (depth/chrome changes) and once at hydrate.
732:  */
733: export function updateNavBackButton(el: HTMLElement, r: DomRenderer): void {
734:   if (!isNavSlot(el) || isCustomChrome(el) || slotDepth(el) <= 1) {
735:     injectedBackButton(el)?.remove();
736:     return;
737:   }
738:   let back = injectedBackButton(el);
739:   if (!back) {
740:     back = document.createElement("button");
741:     back.type = "button";
742:     back.className = NAV_BACK_CLASS;
743:     back.setAttribute("aria-label", "Back");
744:     back.textContent = "‹ Back";
745:     back.addEventListener("click", () => r.onNavigateBack?.());
746:     el.insertBefore(back, el.firstChild); // above the destination
747:   }
748: }
749: 
750: /** Reconcile the default back button for every nav slot in the tree (hydrate). */
751: export function updateNavBackButtons(r: DomRenderer): void {
752:   for (const node of r.byId.values()) {
753:     if (node instanceof HTMLElement && isNavSlot(node)) {
754:       updateNavBackButton(node, r);
755:     }
756:   }
757: }

759: // --- swap transitions (spec DSL.md §4.5 / MODIFIERS.md TRANSITION) ---
760: // When a child is inserted into a slot carrying a `data-pathland-transition` hint,
761: // the DOM client animates the new subtree in (fade/slide/scale). This is a pure
762: // renderer-side animation of its own output cache — never app state.
763: 
764: const TRANSITION_KEYFRAMES: Record<string, string> = {
765:   platform: "@keyframes pl-platform { from { opacity: 0; } to { opacity: 1; } }",
766:   fade: "@keyframes pl-fade { from { opacity: 0; } to { opacity: 1; } }",
767:   slide:
768:     "@keyframes pl-slide { from { opacity: 0; transform: translateX(16px); } to { opacity: 1; transform: none; } }",
769:   scale:
770:     "@keyframes pl-scale { from { opacity: 0; transform: scale(0.96); } to { opacity: 1; transform: none; } }",
771: };
772: 
773: let transitionsInjected = false;
774: 
775: function ensureTransitionStyles(): void {
776:   if (transitionsInjected || typeof document === "undefined") {
777:     return;
778:   }
779:   transitionsInjected = true;
780:   const style = document.createElement("style");
781:   style.setAttribute("data-pathland-transitions", "");
782:   style.textContent = Object.values(TRANSITION_KEYFRAMES).join("\n");
783:   document.head.appendChild(style);
784: }
785: 
786: function maybeAnimateInsert(parent: Node, child: Node): void {
787:   if (!(parent instanceof HTMLElement) || !(child instanceof HTMLElement)) {
788:     return;
789:   }
790:   const name = parent.getAttribute("data-pathland-transition");
791:   if (!name) {
792:     return;
793:   }
794:   ensureTransitionStyles();
795:   const key = TRANSITION_KEYFRAMES[name] ? name : "platform";
796:   child.style.animation = `pl-${key} 180ms ease-out`;
797:   child.addEventListener("animationend", () => {
798:     child.style.animation = "";
799:   }, { once: true });
800: }

802: /** Resolve an element's role shell kind: from the component when known (fresh
803:  *  nodes), else from its tag (SSR-hydrated nodes have no component). */
804: function shellKind(el: HTMLElement): "generic" | "native" | "other" {
805:   const comp = componentByNode.get(el);
806:   if (comp !== undefined) {
807:     if (GENERIC_COMPONENTS.includes(comp)) {
808:       return "generic";
809:     }
810:     if (NATIVE_ROLE_COMPONENTS.includes(comp)) {
811:       return "native";
812:     }
813:     return "other";
814:   }
815:   const t = el.tagName.toLowerCase();
816:   if (t === "div" || t === "span") {
817:     return el.classList.contains("pathland-menu") || el.classList.contains("pathland-stepper")
818:       ? "other"
819:       : "generic";
820:   }
821:   if (
822:     t === "button" ||
823:     t === "input" ||
824:     t === "label" ||
825:     t === "select" ||
826:     t === "textarea" ||
827:     t === "progress" ||
828:     t === "img"
829:   ) {
830:     return "native";
831:   }
832:   return "other";
833: }
834: 
835: /** Replace an element with one of a different tag (a semantic role retag),
836:  *  preserving attributes, children, and the registry entry. */
837: function morphRole(el: HTMLElement, tag: string, r: DomRenderer): HTMLElement {
838:   const fresh = document.createElement(tag);
839:   for (const attr of Array.from(el.attributes)) {
840:     fresh.setAttribute(attr.name, attr.value);
841:   }
842:   while (el.firstChild) {
843:     fresh.appendChild(el.firstChild);
844:   }
845:   if (el.parentNode) {
846:     el.parentNode.replaceChild(fresh, el);
847:   }
848:   const id = Number(el.getAttribute("data-pathland-id"));
849:   if (id) {
850:     r.byId.set(id, fresh);
851:   }
852:   const comp = componentByNode.get(el);
853:   if (comp !== undefined) {
854:     componentByNode.set(fresh, comp);
855:   }
856:   const role = roleByNode.get(el);
857:   if (role !== undefined) {
858:     roleByNode.set(fresh, role);
859:   }
860:   copyTypography(el, fresh);
861:   return fresh;
862: }
863: 
864: /** Resolve and apply the semantic tag + ARIA role for an element from its
865:  *  current `ROLE` / `TEXT_STYLE` state (a heading `TEXT_STYLE` always wins).
866:  *  Retags a generic shell in place when the effective tag differs. */
867: function applySemantic(el: HTMLElement, r: DomRenderer): void {
868:   const kind = shellKind(el);
869:   const role = roleByNode.get(el) ?? 0;
870:   const style = textStyleByNode.get(el);
871:   const tag = textTag(kind, role, style ?? null);
872:   let current = el;
873:   if (tag && current.tagName.toLowerCase() !== tag) {
874:     current = morphRole(current, tag, r);
875:   }
876:   const aria = ariaRole(kind, role);
877:   if (aria) {
878:     current.setAttribute("role", aria);
879:   } else {
880:     current.removeAttribute("role");
881:   }
882: }

884: function applyStyle(op: Opcode, strings: Uint8Array, r: DomRenderer): void {
885:   if (op.command === CMD_SET_DESIGN_TOKEN) {
886:     applyDesignToken(op, strings, (r.tokenSink ??= createTokenSink()));
887:     return;
888:   }
889:   const node = r.byId.get(op.a);
890:   if (!node || node.nodeType !== Node.ELEMENT_NODE) {
891:     return;
892:   }
893:   const el = node as HTMLElement;
894:   switch (op.command) {
895:     case CMD_SET_TEXT:
896:       if (el.classList.contains("pathland-rich-text")) {
897:         el.classList.remove("pathland-rich-text");
898:       }
899:       setNodeText(el, readString(strings, op.b));
900:       break;
901:     case CMD_SET_ATTRIBUTED_TEXT:
902:       applyAttributedText(el, readAttributed(strings, op.b));
903:       break;
904:     case CMD_SET_DATE: {
905:       const input = el.matches("input[type=date],input[type=time],input[type=datetime-local]")
906:         ? (el as HTMLInputElement)
907:         : el.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>("input[type=date],input[type=time],input[type=datetime-local]");
908:       if (input) {
909:         if (input.type === "time") {
910:           input.value = millisToTime(op.c);
911:         } else if (input.type === "datetime-local") {
912:           const date = daysToIso(op.b);
913:           const time = millisToTime(op.c);
914:           input.value = date ? `${date}T${time}` : time;
915:         } else {
916:           input.value = daysToIso(op.b);
917:         }
918:       }
919:       break;
920:     }
921:     case CMD_SET_PROPERTY: {
922:       const propId = op.b & 0xffff;
923:       const valueType = (op.b >>> 16) & 0xff;
924:       if (valueType === VAL_STRING) {
925:         const text = readString(strings, op.c);
926:         if (propId === PROP_ROUTE) {
927:           el.setAttribute("data-pathland-route", text);
928:           r.onRoute?.(text); // host mirrors the URL (history.pushState)
929:         } else {
930:           applyStringProperty(el, propId, text);
931:           if (propId === PROP_MEDIA_SOURCE) {
932:             // A controller's resource: wire its playback element + listeners
933:             // (spec/MEDIA.md) and resume playback if the app was playing (a src
934:             // change pauses the element). A controller is non-visual — it never
935:             // renders native controls.
936:             ensureMediaElement(el, propId);
937:             applyStringProperty(el, propId, text);
938:             setupMediaElement(el, r);

Let me enumerate concerns in the issue:
1. WS origin checks — Spring setAllowedOrigins("*"), Quarkus default? Need origin check.

3. no CSRF/CSP/SRI — SSR HTML needs CSP and SRI? The bundle is same-origin content-hashed. SRI requires integrity attr for script tags. CSP.
4. rate limit — WS message rate limits.
5. JS decoder bounds (applyBatch/readString), per-opcode validation — parseBatch mostly bounds-checked; readString checked; readList checked; attributed checked. But potential integer overflow in `opcodesEnd = HEADER_SIZE + opcodeCount*OPCODE_SIZE` (JS numbers safe for u32*16 ~ 6.8e10 < 2^53, fine) and `start + len` where len up to 2^32, start up to length—safe. Per-opcode validation: component IDs, property value types, etc. Also DoS: opcodeCount up to 4 billion would allocate huge array before truncation check? In JS no. But `new Array(count)` with count up to 2^32 could allocate huge before bounds check? Bounds check is before allocation: `if (start + count*4 > strings.length) throw`. Fine.

Potential issue: `parseBatch` doesn't check trailing bytes, header flags. `readString` offset from op.c could be arbitrary; checked. But applyBatch exceptions rethrow causing whole client to fail; maybe catch and reset. Not security.

133:       clearInterval(this.pingTimer);

135:     }

139:     }
140:   }

142:   private connect(): void {
143:     log.debug("ws", "connecting", this.options.url);
144:     const ws = this.options.createSocket
145:       ? this.options.createSocket(this.options.url)
146:       : new WebSocket(this.options.url);
147:     this.ws = ws;
148:     ws.binaryType = "arraybuffer";
149:     ws.onopen = () => {
150:       // A reconnect means the client missed deltas while disconnected: request a
151:       // full snapshot (META::RESYNC). The first connect never does — the client
152:       // already has the whole UI from the SSR HTML. On EVERY open (before any
153:       // resync) the client sends its environment (viewport + route).
154:       this.lastActivityAt = Date.now();
155:       // Re-baseline the sequence on the next guest → host batch (a fresh
156:       // connection's stream restarts; see §Sequence gap detection).
157:       this.expectedSequence = null;
158:       const reconnected = this.attempt > 0;
159:       this.attempt = 0;
160:       log.info("ws", reconnected ? "connected (reconnect)" : "connected");
161:       this.options.onStatus?.("open");
162:       this.options.onOpen?.(this);

165:         this.send(encodeResync());
166:       }
167:     };
168:     ws.onmessage = (event) => this.handleMessage(event.data);
169:     ws.onerror = () => {
170:       log.error("ws", "socket error");
171:       // onclose always follows; nothing to do here.
172:     };
173:     ws.onclose = () => {
174:       this.ws = null;
175:       if (this.stopped) {
176:         log.debug("ws", "closed (stopped)");
177:         return;
178:       }
179:       log.info("ws", "closed — reconnecting (attempt", this.attempt + 1 + ")");
180:       this.options.onStatus?.("reconnecting");
181:       this.scheduleReconnect();
182:     };

185:   private scheduleReconnect(): void {
186:     if (this.attempt >= MAX_ATTEMPTS) {
187:       return;
188:     }
189:     const delay = Math.min(BASE_DELAY_MS * 2 ** this.attempt, MAX_DELAY_MS);
190:     this.attempt++;

192:   }

194:   private handleMessage(data: unknown): void {
195:     // Any server batch (a delta, a META::PONG, anything) proves the connection
196:     // is alive — reset the heartbeat watchdog.
197:     this.lastActivityAt = Date.now();
198:     let bytes: Uint8Array;
199:     if (data instanceof ArrayBuffer) {

201:     } else if (data instanceof Blob) {
202:       // A Blob read can abort (socket close / navigation) — swallow it rather than
203:       // surface an unhandled promise rejection.
204:       data.arrayBuffer()
205:         .then((buffer) => this.handleMessage(buffer))
206:         .catch(() => undefined);
207:       return;
208:     } else {
209:       bytes = new Uint8Array(0);
210:     }
211:     let batch: Batch;
212:     try {
213:       batch = parseBatch(bytes);
214:     } catch (err) {
215:       if (err instanceof ProtocolError) {
216:         log.error("ws", "rejected batch:", err.message);
217:         return;
218:       }
219:       throw err;
220:     }
221:     log.info("ws", "← recv", describeBatch(batch));
222:     log.debug("ws", "← recv detail", describeBatchDetail(batch));

224:       log.warn("ws", `protocol version ${batch.version} != ${VERSION}; reloading`);
225:       location.reload();
226:       return;
227:     }

229:     // guest → host delta batch whose sequence breaks the chain means one or more
230:     // batches were lost while the socket stayed open. Do not apply the gapped
231:     // batch (its deltas assume the lost state); request a full snapshot and
232:     // re-baseline on the next batch.
233:     if (this.isSequenceGap(batch)) {
234:       log.warn(
235:         "ws",
236:         `sequence gap: expected ${this.expectedSequence}, got ${batch.sequence} — requesting RESYNC`,
237:       );
238:       this.expectedSequence = null;
239:       this.send(encodeResync());
240:       return;
241:     }
242:     this.trackSequence(batch);
243:     try {
244:       applyBatch(batch, this.options.renderer);
245:     } catch (err) {
246:       if (err instanceof ProtocolError) {
247:         log.error("ws", "rejected delta:", err.message);
248:         return;
249:       }
250:       throw err;
251:     }
252:     this.options.onBatch?.(batch);

257:    * Host → guest batches (heartbeat `PONG`, request echoes) carry sequence 0 and
258:    * are not part of the guest → host stream, so they are ignored here.
259:    */
260:   private isSequenceGap(batch: Batch): boolean {
261:     if ((batch.flags & FLAG_HOST_TO_GUEST) !== 0) {
262:       return false;
263:     }
264:     return this.expectedSequence !== null && batch.sequence !== this.expectedSequence;
265:   }

267:   /** Advance the expected sequence from a guest → host delta batch (baseline or next). */
268:   private trackSequence(batch: Batch): void {
269:     if ((batch.flags & FLAG_HOST_TO_GUEST) !== 0) {
270:       return;
271:     }
272:     this.expectedSequence = batch.sequence + 1;
273:   }

289:   isReload: boolean,
290:   urlHadWid: boolean,
291:   ssrScoped: boolean,
292: ): boolean {

parts.text:
So no cookie in current code. The issue is partly stale. But we can still plan for current relevant surfaces: WS origin checks, rate limit, CSP + SRI, JS bounds/per-opcode validation. Possibly CSRF irrelevant for WS given origin check; but CSRF for SSR/actions? There are no state-changing HTTP endpoints except WS. CSRF protection for WebSocket = Origin header check. Could also add SameSite cookie? no cookies.

Wait — maybe the issue was filed when cookies existed. It's still open. We could note that cookie flags are N/A now because per-window identity moved to sessionStorage, but to be safe: if any cookie is introduced, flags. Or implement an optional cookie? Not necessary.

Let's thoroughly assess:

1. WS origin checks:
- Spring: `setAllowedOrigins("*")` allows cross-origin WebSocket connections. Need configurable allowed origins, default same-origin (no origins? Spring default if not set is same origin? Spring's default is same-origin when not set). Provide property `pathland.allowed-origins` (comma list) or derive from request. Setting `.setAllowedOrigins()` with no args defaults to same-origin? Spring's `WebSocketHandlerRegistration#setAllowedOrigins(String...)` — by default only same-origin allowed unless configured. So remove `*` and use property. But same-origin check in Spring derives from `Origin` and host. Need consider reverse proxies; allow config.
- Quarkus websockets-next: origin checking config? Quarkus has `quarkus.websockets-next.server.allowed-origins` maybe? Let me check knowledge: Quarkus WebSockets Next has CORS/origin? I'm not certain. There may be `quarkus.websockets-next.server.auto-ping-interval` etc. Origin check? Could implement in `@OnOpen` by reading `connection.handshakeRequest().header("Origin")` and compare to Host/X-Forwarded-Host, or config. But also must close/reject connection. In websockets-next, can we abort? Maybe throw `WebSocketServerException`? Or close with `connection.close()`? Need investigate. Alternatively add a Vert.x filter for the WS handshake paths that checks Origin on the HTTP upgrade. That's robust and works for both root and mounted sockets: `Filters` / reactive route. A Quarkus HTTP filter can inspect `Upgrade: websocket` and `Origin` and reject with 403. This would handle both endpoints. Good.

2. Session cookie: currently none; document as N/A / remove. But perhaps there is a widening: if a future cookie, set `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax`. We can add a note. Or maybe the issue wants us to keep `wid` out of URL; it's already in sessionStorage. We could also bind the wid to a signed cookie to prevent state hijacking? Not exactly. The wid is user-controlled and is a state scope; an attacker guessing another user's wid could read their state via SSR `?wid=` or ws. That's a real security issue! `renderHtml(route, windowId)` honors `?wid=` from the query string for SSR. The client strips stale wid, but the server accepts any wid from query. The WS likewise accepts any `wid`. So persisted state is scoped by a client-provided, unauthenticated UUID. If an attacker learns/guesses a wid (UUID v4 = unguessable), they can access its state. That's capability-based; UUID random is okay-ish but state can be accessed cross-window if the wid leaks (referrer, logs, etc.). Since wid is only in WS URL and sessionStorage, it won't leak via referrer. But the SSR path does accept `?wid=` for stale/bookmarked URLs (legacy), creating a capability in the URL. Security hardening could:
   - Stop accepting `?wid=` on SSR entirely? But they deliberately keep it for stale links + tests. Hmm.
   - Bind wid to a signed cookie? The issue says non-HttpOnly session cookie. Maybe intended design: use HttpOnly cookie for session identity, not sessionStorage. That would be a bigger change. But current architecture explicitly avoids cookies. We should not upend architecture without user direction.

Let me ask the user what scope they want? The task: "Lets plan a fix for #63". We should produce a plan. We can note stale parts and propose. Maybe use question tool to clarify whether to include a cookie-based session identity or treat cookie item as obsolete. But maybe better to inspect issue timeline/author intent. Let me fetch issue details via gh (createdAt, author).

Issue created Sept 2026, current date Nov 2026. The cookie thing likely from an older architecture at that point? But the current code (Nov) shows sessionStorage. Maybe in Sept there was a session cookie and it was later removed. So cookie part now obsolete. But the issue asks broadly. Let's plan comprehensively but flag obsolete.

Need also consider CSP and SRI. Since SSR HTML is generated by the Rust renderer and then hosts inject script. Approaches:
- Add CSP header at host level (Spring/Quarkus) rather than in HTML? For script-src 'self' and maybe 'unsafe-inline' for inline styles (the SSR emits inline style attributes and `<style>` elements). CSP style-src 'unsafe-inline' required. Script only external bundle, so `script-src 'self'` works. But service worker registration requires worker-src 'self'. Media/image/font etc. `default-src 'self'`, `img-src 'self' data:` (icons maybe inline? check), `media-src 'self'`, `connect-src 'self' ws: wss:` (for WebSocket). Add `frame-ancestors 'none'`, `object-src 'none'`, `base-uri 'self'`. Need support configured asset origins? Proxy? asset-dir same-origin. Possibly `data:` for image? Let's inspect inline SVG usage. `img-src 'self' data:` safe enough. But CSP applies to SSR HTML only; the WS/asset responses don't need it.
- Configurable CSP property; default enforce or report-only? For a reference implementation, default enforce with safe directives. But inline styles means `style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'`, which is a known weakness but necessary due to inline styles in the protocol. Could add nonce for `<style>`? But inline style attributes can't be nonce'd. CSP3 `style-src-attr 'unsafe-inline'` could restrict style elements. But the renderer emits `<style data-pathland-tokens>` and fit. Could nonce those, but separate. Simpler: `style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'`. Document.
- SRI: script tag references a content-hashed bundle served immutable. Add `integrity="sha384-..."` and `crossorigin="anonymous"`? For same-origin, SRI works without crossorigin. The server (PathlandSession) needs the bundle's digest. PathlandAssets currently reads only the filename from manifest. We could generate a `.sha384` manifest or compute hash at startup from classpath. Since bundle is content-hashed, its URL is already integrity-busting, but SRI protects against server-side tampering? SRI's threat model is compromised CDN. Still issue asks SRI. Add to PathlandAssets: read bundle bytes and base64 SHA-384 once, cache; emit `integrity="sha384-…"`. But pathland-server-core may not know the resource path (it currently only knows name; resource in static/_pathland/). We can extend the manifest to include integrity? Simpler: extend the pointer manifest to two lines: filename + sha384 base64. The TS copy script can compute. Let me inspect the copy script.

<content>
1: // Copy the built bundle into both demo modules' static resource dirs so the
2: // Maven jars stay self-contained and both demos serve the SAME artifact. The
3: // bundle lives under the reserved framework prefix `/_pathland/` (spec).
4: //
5: // The served filename carries a sha-256 content hash (`dom-renderer-<hash>.js`)
6: // so a new bundle always changes the URL — the scripts are served with
7: // `immutable` cache headers, and a fresh name is the only thing that busts the
8: // cache. A tiny pointer manifest `dom-renderer.current` (one line, the current
9: // hashed filename) is written next to the copies so the SSR layer emits the
10: // right <script src> without re-hashing. Stale `dom-renderer-*.js` (and the
11: // pre-hash fixed `dom-renderer.js`) are pruned so the dirs never accumulate.
12: import { createHash } from "node:crypto";
13: import { copyFileSync, mkdirSync, readFileSync, readdirSync, rmSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
14: import { dirname, join, resolve } from "node:path";
15: import { fileURLToPath } from "node:url";
16: 
17: const root = resolve(dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)), "..");
18: const source = resolve(root, "dist/pathland-dom-renderer.js");
19: const bundle = readFileSync(source);
20: const hash = createHash("sha256").update(bundle).digest("hex").slice(0, 12);
21: const name = `dom-renderer-${hash}.js`;
22: const manifest = "dom-renderer.current";
23: 
24: const targets = [
25:   resolve(root, "../java/pathland-quarkus-demo/src/main/resources/META-INF/resources/_pathland"),
26:   resolve(root, "../java/pathland-spring-boot-demo/src/main/resources/static/_pathland"),
27: ];
28: 
29: for (const dir of targets) {
30:   mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true });
31: 
32:   for (const entry of readdirSync(dir)) {
33:     if (entry === name || entry === manifest) continue;
34:     if (!entry.startsWith("dom-renderer-") && entry !== "dom-renderer.js") continue;
35:     rmSync(join(dir, entry));
36:     console.log(`pruned stale ${entry} <- ${dir.replace(root, "…")}/`);
37:   }
38: 
39:   const dest = resolve(dir, name);
40:   copyFileSync(source, dest);
41:   console.log(`copied -> ${dest.replace(root, "…")}`);
42: 
43:   writeFileSync(resolve(dir, manifest), name + "\n");
44:   console.log(`wrote   -> ${resolve(dir, manifest).replace(root, "…")}`);
45: 
46:   // The per-window-id service worker (issue #155) is copied verbatim under a STABLE
47:   // name: the browser re-fetches it to byte-compare for updates, so it must NOT be
48:   // content-hashed (unlike the bundle) and is served `no-cache`.
49:   copyFileSync(resolve(root, "sw.js"), resolve(dir, "sw.js"));
50:   console.log(`copied -> ${resolve(dir, "sw.js").replace(root, "…")}`);
51: }

We need to decide semantics: reject entire batch on unknown category/command? Or ignore unknown opcodes? For forward compatibility, unknown opcodes should be ignored (renderer already defaults). But security: prevent prototype pollution / DOM clobbering / huge operations. Potential dangers in apply:
- `op.a`/`op.b` are numbers read via `r.byId.get`, users can't inject other types.
- `CMD_SET_PROPERTY` val string `PROP_IMAGE_SOURCE` sets `img.src` to arbitrary URL (e.g., javascript:? img src won't execute JS; data: could). Not a security boundary because server controls the stream. The threat model is a malicious server? Usually XSS from server-provided content is still relevant (stored XSS). But protocol app controls content; rendering text via textContent is safe. Link hrefs from attributed text could be `javascript:`. Should sanitize URLs (link href, image src, media src). CSP helps.
- `applyAttributedText`: creates `<a href=...>` from link URL. `javascript:` link is XSS on click. Need URL scheme allowlist.
- `setIcon`: fetches icons.
- `readString`/`readList` bounds already there but potential integer overflow in `start + len` in JS no; but `offset` might be negative? Reads are unsigned u32, so nonnegative. `offset + 4 > strings.length` fine.
- `parseBatch`: unvalidated `opcodeCount` check multiplication safe (<2^53). `sequence` etc.
- `readAttributed`: need(12) before reading, good. But offsets start/end aren't validated against textBytes length; attributedSegments adds out-of-range boundaries and creates subarray with clamping? `value.textBytes.subarray(segment.start, segment.end)` clamps automatically; but could produce weird empty. Not a security issue beyond large sets. Could validate.

"Per-opcode validation" maybe meant the Rust decoders? Issue #38 covers Rust strict bounds. This #63 is web. The JS applyBatch/readString already has bounds. Maybe the issue predates those fixes; we should verify tests and add negative tests. Let's check git log for plpl hardening.

We can add per-opcode validation: category/command knowledge, value type validation, node existence, string ref bounds before side effects. Currently applyStyle reads string after getting node; if node missing it returns without reading string (fine). For SET_ATTRIBUTED_TEXT reads string. Rejects ProtocolError. The transport catches ProtocolError in applyBatch? Yes handleMessage catches ProtocolError around applyBatch and logs. Good.

But a malicious opcode can still do weird: `CMD_MOVE_CHILD` with a=child b=; insertAt guards cycles. Good.

Rate limiting: server-side per-connection event rate/budget. PathlandRegistry has MAX_EVENT_BATCH size only. Add token-bucket/limited queue: track per-session last-seen / event counts per window, drop or close when exceeding. Must be careful not to break legitimate interactions. Configurable: `pathland.max-event-batch` already 64K; add `pathland.event-rate-per-second` default e.g. 200 events/s, `pathland.event-burst` e.g. 400. Or a simple per-connection counter window in registry (on actor thread) and telemetry. Also inbound connection count limits? The issue says "rate limit" generally. Could also rate-limit WS connections (handshake) per IP with filter. Simpler to do per-session event budget plus max sessions? Need scope.

CSRF: WebSocket CSRF is mitigated by Origin check. HTTP SSR is GET only (no state change), no cookies. So no CSRF token necessary. Note in plan.

CSP/SRI: as above.

WS Origin checks: Both frameworks. Need configurable allowed origins with defaults. For a BFF, often behind proxy with same origin. Implementation:
- Add a shared helper in server-core e.g. `OriginPolicy` to parse `Origin` vs `Host`/`X-Forwarded-Host`? But HTTP framework integration differs. We can expose `pathland.allowed-origins` property consumed by starter/extension. Spring: inject property into `pathlandWebSocketConfigurer`, call `.setAllowedOrigins(origins)`; default empty -> same origin. Could also support wildcard patterns `setAllowedOriginPatterns`. For Quarkus: add `OriginCheckFilter` that checks `Upgrade: websocket` and any `/_pathland/ws` path against config `pathland.allowed-origins` (default same-host). Need to get host. With reverse proxy, use `X-Forwarded-Host` only if trusted proxies configured (Quarkus has `quarkus.http.proxy.proxy-address-forwarding=true`). We can rely on Vert.x normalized host and scheme. For Spring, Spring does origin check itself using request host. With `ForwardedHeaderFilter` etc. Document.

Potential issue: Spring `setAllowedOrigins("*")` with credentials? no. Remove.

Maybe also validate WS handshake `wid`: bound length and charset; currently `wid` could be arbitrarily long (query string). `stateScope` includes it in map keys/store keys. A huge wid can bloat memory. Add validation: UUID-ish? The client sends a UUID, but tests use `w1`, `sessA`, `shared-wid`. We can cap length (e.g. 128) and allowed chars `[A-Za-z0-9._:-]`, else generate fresh. Also SSR `wid` param same validation. That's a good object-level hardening and addresses "per-window state" safety. Could even sign it? Not now.

Also query param decoding: `queryParam` doesn't URL-decode; wid is a UUID so fine; but Spring/Quarkus both parse raw. Client `crypto.randomUUID()` no special chars. But tests use normal. Validate.

CSP + SRI mechanics:
- Add `PathlandAssets.bundleBytes()`? PathlandSession can compute SRI itself if the bundle is on the classpath. Extend `PathlandAssets` with `bundleIntegrity()` reading manifest second line or reading resource. Better: update copy script to write `dom-renderer.current` as `name\nsha384-<base64>\n`. But tests for resolve expect first line only; add second line support and fallback (compute from resource if second line absent). Simpler: PathlandAssets reads the manifest first line name, then opens `static/_pathland/<name>` (or META-INF/resources/...) and computes SHA-384. But computing on each SSR call expensive; cache. PathlandAssets has a lookup mechanism; could add `openBundle` to lookup paths with `META-INF/resources/_pathland/`, `static/_pathland/`, `_pathland/`. Then at startup read bytes, hash. Add `bundleIntegrity()`. If missing, omit integrity. Tests can validate. This avoids changing manifest format/CI. However, in Spring demo the bundle is on classpath; Quarkus too. In library-only fallback `dom-renderer.js` may not exist -> no integrity.
- Emit `<script src="..." integrity="sha384-..." defer></script>`. Note `crossorigin="anonymous"` not required for same-origin, and would trigger CORS if assets served from same origin anyway fine. Better omit. SRI requires CORS for cross-origin only; same origin works.

CSP header:
- Spring: add a `OncePerRequestFilter` / set headers in `PathlandIndexController` responses. But CSP should apply to SSR HTML; easiest to set `Content-Security-Policy` in `index()` response only. Could add a bean property. However other static assets responses shouldn't need CSP. Also `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`? `frame-ancestors` covers embedding.
- Quarkus: add to `render()` response header, or a global filter for HTML. Since `IndexResource` returns Response, add `.header("Content-Security-Policy", ...)`. But mounted app paths route through same resource. Good.
- Configurable: `pathland.csp` property to override; default policy. Quarkus extension config? Currently Quarkus extension has config? Let's inspect for `@ConfigProperty` usage / ConfigRoot.

The status explicitly says "Per-window isolation (no session cookie)... The old `session` cookie is removed." So the issue's cookie item is definitely obsolete. Good—we'll note as resolved/N/A.

state.output:
connection seam (default: the JDK `HttpClient` WebSocket client, no new dependency) with a `Factory` so a starter can swap a native client. - **`proxy.ProxySession`** — one origin connection: sends `META::ENVIRONMENT` + `META::RESYNC`, **remaps** the origin snapshot into the proxy's block and attaches the origin root under the proxy node, forwards live deltas remapped, routes client events back (target unmapped), replies `PONG` to origin `PING`, translates origin `META::RESET` into a **scoped** subtree teardown (never a global reset), tears the subtree down on disconnect (the origin session is per-connection), and reconnects with exponential backoff. While an SSR snapshot is pending, `awaitSnapshot` retries `META::RESYNC` every 500 ms, so a lost first handshake cannot consume the whole SSR budget. The service credential + a cycle-guard instance id ride the handshake headers. **Backpressure** (spec/PROXY.md §8): a "chatty origin" breaker (a per-second batch cap → drop + `RESYNC`) and event coalescing (pointer-moves coalesce by target; discrete events flush immediately). - **`proxy.ProxyHost`** — one `ProxySession` per `PROXY_VIEW` node, each with its own block; routes inbound events whose target is in a proxy range to the owning origin connection; owns the proxy scheduler. `reconcile(wanted)` starts a session for every `PROXY_VIEW` node and closes the session of every node that left the tree; released id blocks go to a **free-block pool** and are reused, so repeated removal/re-add cycles never exhaust the 1024-block range. - **`PathlandSession`** integration — captures `RenderResult.proxyViews()` and registers the emitter's structural-reconcile callback (`Emitter.onStructureReconciled`) to `reconcileProxies()`, so a proxy lives **exactly while its node is in the retained tree** (spec/PROXY.md §7): a `SizeThatFits` slot dropping the candidate that held it closes the origin connection, and re-adding it opens a fresh one (re-seeded by `META::RESYNC`). Let me formulate succinctly but complete.

## Findings

- `setAllowedOrigins("*")` is real: `PathlandAutoConfiguration.java:124`.
- The “non-HttpOnly session cookie” item is **obsolete**: there is no session cookie anymore. Per-window identity is `wid` in `sessionStorage`, sent only on the WS URL (`lib/java/pathland-server-core/status.md` explicitly records “no session cookie”).
- No CSP, no SRI, no security headers today. SSR injects the bundle here: `PathlandSession.java:374`.
- JS decoding is mostly bounds-checked already (`plpl.ts`), but lacks batch-size caps, per-opcode validation, atomic validation, URL sanitization, and node-count bounds.
- I found an additional **critical server-side decoder bug**: `FrameCodec.parse` (`FrameCodec.kt:244`) does `Int` arithmetic on the attacker-controlled `opcodeCount`. A 20-byte message with `opcodeCount=0x20000000` overflows `opcodeCount * 16` to 0, passes the bounds check, then `ArrayList(536M)` OOMs the server. The `MAX_EVENT_BATCH` cap does not protect this because it checks message size, not the declared count.
- Rate limiting today is only `MAX_EVENT_BATCH` size (`PathlandRegistry.java:53`); there is no per-session event-rate cap.

## Proposed plan

### 1. Decoder hardening (highest severity)

**Java (`FrameCodec.kt`)**
- Parse `opcodeCount`/`stringsLen` as unsigned and compute offsets with `Long`.
- Reject `opcodeCount`/`stringsLen` before allocating and before any array copy; cap both by remaining bytes.
- Add bounds checks in `Parsed.stringAt` and `decodeEnvironment`.
- Add adversarial tests: overflowing `opcodeCount`, negative/huge `stringsLen`, truncated string offsets, trailing garbage.

**TypeScript (`plpl.ts`, `apply.ts`, `transport.ts`)**
- Add hard caps: `MAX_OPCODES`, `MAX_STRING_BYTES`, `MAX_LIST_COUNT`, `MAX_RUNS`, `MAX_LINKS`, `MAX_ATTRS`, `MAX_NODES`.
- Add a structural `validateBatch()` pass **before** applying any mutation, so a malformed batch cannot leave a half-applied DOM; invalid batches throw `ProtocolError` → host drops/requests `RESYNC`.
- Validate attributed-text ranges (`start <= end <= textLen`) and URLs; add `safeHref`/`safeSrc` allowlists blocking `javascript:` and non-image `data:` URLs.
- Bound inbound WS message size in `transport.handleMessage`; close/resync after repeated invalid batches.
- Tests for every negative vector.

### 2. WebSocket origin checks / CSRF

**Spring**
- Replace the wildcard with a configurable `pathland.allowed-origins` list; default = same-origin (Spring’s default when `setAllowedOrigins` is not wildcard).
- Add optional `pathland.ws.allowed-origin-patterns` for subdomains.
- Tests: same-origin accepted, `https://evil.example` rejected.

**Quarkus**
- Add a `WsOriginFilter` (`Vert.x Filters`) matching `/_pathland/ws` and `/{app}/_pathland/ws`:
  - when `Origin` is present, require it to match request scheme+authority or an explicit `pathland.allowed-origins` entry;
  - reject with `403` otherwise.
- Default: same-origin; missing `Origin` allowed (non-browser clients) unless `pathland.ws.require-origin=true`.
- Update `WsSession` test harness to send an `Origin` header; add a rejection test.

**CSRF**
- No CSRF tokens needed: SSR is GET-only, no cookies exist, and WS mutations are protected by the origin check. Document this rationale in the status files.

### 3. Rate limiting and identity bounds

- Add a per-session inbound event breaker in `PathlandSession.dispatch` (same pattern as the proxy “chatty origin” breaker): batches/events per second, configurable via `pathland.max-event-batches-per-second` (default 2000) and `pathland.max-events-per-second`.
- On breach: drop the batch, log, emit a new `PathlandTelemetry.eventBatchDropped(mount, reason)` + Micrometer counter.
- Make `MAX_EVENT_BATCH` configurable (`pathland.max-event-batch-bytes`, default 64 KiB).
- Validate `wid` centrally (length ≤ 128, `[A-Za-z0-9._-]`); invalid `wid` becomes a fresh UUID / SSR defaults. This prevents unbounded or colliding state-store keys.
- Optional: close after sustained abuse (e.g. N consecutive dropped batches); propose drop-only first to avoid reconnect storms.

### 4. CSP + SRI + security headers

- **SRI**: update `copy-to-demos.mjs` to write `name\nsha384-<base64>` into `dom-renderer.current`; extend `PathlandAssets` to expose `bundleIntegrity()` (parse second line, fall back to runtime SHA-384 of the bundle, omit if unavailable). Emit `integrity="sha384-…"` on the SSR script tag.
- **CSP**: add a shared default in `pathland-server-core`:
  ```text
  default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline';
  img-src 'self' data:; media-src 'self'; font-src 'self';
  connect-src 'self' ws: wss:; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self';
  form-action 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; worker-src 'self'
  ```
  `style-src 'unsafe-inline'` is required because the protocol emits inline styles/`<style data-pathland-tokens>`.
- Add `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`.
- Apply to SSR HTML in Spring (`PathlandIndexController`) and Quarkus (`IndexResource`), with an override property `pathland.content-security-policy` (supports report-only if desired).
- Add header assertions to both starter test suites.

### 5. Status/docs/verification

- Update `pathland-server-core/status.md`, `pathland-spring-boot-starter/status.md`, `pathland-quarkus/status.md`, `lib/typescript/status.md`.
- Add a short “Security” section to `README.md` covering origin policy, CSP/SRI, rate limits, and the intentional absence of a session cookie/CSRF tokens.
- Verify:
  - `cd lib/typescript && npm run typecheck && npm test`
  - `cd lib/rust && cargo test`
  - `cd lib/java && mvn install` (after `cargo build -p pathland-render-html -p pathland-markdown-capi`)

## Suggested sequencing

1. **PR 1**: decoder hardening (Java + JS) — fixes the OOM/DoS.
2. **PR 2**: WS origin checks + rate limiting + `wid` validation.
3. **PR 3**: CSP + SRI + security headers + docs/status.

## Decisions I’d take unless you prefer otherwise

- Treat the cookie item as resolved/N/A (no cookie exists).
- Default CSP is **enforcing**, with a `pathland.content-security-policy` override.
- Default WS policy is **same-origin**, missing `Origin` allowed for non-browser clients.
- Rate-limit default: 2000 batches/s and 20k events/s per session, drop-only.

Highlights:
# Quarkus Bucket4j

Bucket4J is a Java rate-limiting library based on the token-bucket algorithm. Bucket4j is a thread-safe library that can be used in either a standalone JVM application, or a clustered environment. It also supports in-memory or distributed caching via the JCache (JSR107) specification. This extension allow you to control the request rate sent to your application by using a dead simple API.

## Installation

If you want to use this extension, you need to add the `io.quarkiverse.bucket4j:quarkus-bucket4j` extension first to your build file.

For instance, with Maven, add the following dependency to your POM file:

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.quarkiverse.bucket4j</groupId>
    <artifactId>quarkus-bucket4j</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.7</version>
</dependency>
```

## Getting Started

### Throttling a Method

Annotate the method that need to be throttled with @RateLimited

```java
@ApplicationScoped
public static class RateLimitedMethods {

    @RateLimited(bucket = "group1")
    public String limited() {
        return "LIMITED";
    }

}
```

The annotation is repeatable enabling to set multiple limit, in such case, any exhausted bucket lead to the failure of the call.

```java
@ApplicationScoped
public static class RateLimitedMethods {

    @RateLimited(bucket = "group1")
    @RateLimited(bucket = "group2")
    public String limited() {
        return "LIMITED";
    }

}
```

You can also annotate a class, in that case all methods in the class are throttled

```java
@ApplicationScoped
@RateLimited(bucket = "group1")
public static class RateLimitedMethods {

    public String limited() {
        return "LIMITED";
    }

}
```

Method level annotation overrides class level annotation. In the example bellow:

- `method1` is throttled by bucket `group1`
- `method2` is throttled by bucket `group2`

```java
@ApplicationScoped
@RateLimited(bucket = "group1")
public static class RateLimitedMethods {

    public String method1() {
        return "LIMITED";
    }

    @RateLimited(bucket = "group2")
    public String method2() {
        return "LIMITED";
    }

}
```

And add a limit group using the same bucket id in the configuration:

```properties
# burst protection
quarkus.rate-limiter.buckets.group1.limits[0].permitted-uses: 10
quarkus.rate-limiter.buckets.group1.limits[0].period: 1S
# fair use
quarkus.rate-limiter.buckets.group1.limits[1].permitted-uses: 100
quarkus.rate-limiter.buckets.group1.limits[1].period: 5M
```

or with yaml:

```yaml
quarkus:
  rate-limiter:
    buckets:
      group1:
        limits:
          - permitted-uses: 10
            period: 1S
          - permitted-uses: 100
            period: 5M
```

The bucket can contain multiple limits that will all be enforced.

### Bucket Sharing

By default, if multiple methods share the same bucket id, each method has its own quota. You can change this behaviour by enabling the shared option in the configuration.

```properties
# burst protection
quarkus.rate-limiter.buckets.group1.shared: true
quarkus.rate-limiter.buckets.group1.limits[0].permitted-uses: 10
quarkus.rate-limiter.buckets.group1.limits[0].period: 1S
```

### Population Segmentation

If you want to perform the throttling per user, simply specify an IdentityKeyResolver either in the bucket config or in the RateLimited annotation. If a value is specified in the annotation, it will take precedence over the config. The default one is the ConstantResolver, which will cause the segmentation to be disabled.

```java
@ApplicationScoped
public static class RateLimitedMethods {
```

Title: Mastering API Throttling in Java: Build a Smart, Tier-Aware Rate Limiter with Quarkus and Bucket4j
URL: https://www.the-main-thread.com/p/smart-api-rate-limiting-quarkus-bucket4j
Published: 2025-06-22T06:08:24.000Z
Author: Markus Eisele
Highlights:
# Mastering API Throttling in Java: Build a Smart, Tier-Aware Rate Limiter with Quarkus and Bucket4j

### From FREE to PRO tenants. Learn how to dynamically control access to your APIs using custom annotations and the full power of Bucket4j in a Quarkus application.

Markus Eisele

Jun 22, 2025

Rate limiting is one of those things you don’t think about until your API gets hammered. Whether you’re building a public SaaS platform, offering free developer access, or protecting resource-heavy operations in a multi-tenant backend, rate limiting is essential. Without it, a single misbehaving client, or a coordinated attack, can drag your system to its knees.

API abuse is real. From noisy neighbors on a shared tier to overzealous bots hammering endpoints—an unguarded API can spell disaster for stability and cost. That’s where rate limiting shines, especially in multi-tenant SaaS systems where fairness and tier-based restrictions are essential.

In this hands-on guide, we’ll build CloudMetrics, a pretend SaaS API offering performance metrics and reports. Along the way, we’ll add intelligent rate-limiting using both the Bucket4j Quarkus extension and a more dynamic version directly using Bucket4j APIs, powered by the blazing-fast Quarkus framework.

Let’s go from basic global throttling to tenant-aware logic and subscription-tier enforcement.

What You’ll Learn

- How to set up a Quarkus REST API with Bucket4j
- How to apply global rate limits
- How to implement per-tenant rate limiting using request headers
- How to build a dynamic, tier-based rate limit system (Free vs. Pro)
- How to combine multiple limits (burst + sustained)

...

Start by creating a fresh Quarkus project with REST and Bucket4j support.

```
mvn io.quarkus.platform:quarkus-maven-plugin:create \
    -DprojectGroupId=com.cloudmetrics \
    -DprojectArtifactId=cloud-metrics \
    -DclassName="com.cloudmetrics.api.MetricsResource" \
    -Dpath="/metrics" \
    -Dextensions="rest-jackson,quarkus-bucket4j"
cd cloud-metrics

...

Nice. Let’s rate limit this thing.

Global Rate Limit

Our CPU metrics endpoint is very lightweight. Let's apply a simple, global rate limit to it: no more than 5 requests every 10 seconds for everyone combined.

In `MetricsResource.java`, annotate the method:

```
import io.quarkiverse.bucket4j.runtime.RateLimited;

@GET
@Path("/metrics/cpu")
@RateLimited(bucket = "cpu-metrics-limit")
public String getCpuMetrics() {
    return "CPU usage: 42%";
}
```

Now, define the bucket named cpu-metrics-limit in your `application.properties` file.

```
quarkus.rate-limiter.buckets.cpu-metrics-limit.limits[0].permitted-uses=5
quarkus.rate-limiter.buckets.cpu-metrics-limit.limits[0].period=10S
```

- permitted-uses=5: The bucket holds 5 tokens.
- period=10S: The bucket is refilled with 5 tokens every 10 seconds.

...

Per-Tenant Rate Limiting

In a SaaS world, you don’t punish one tenant for another’s traffic. Let's isolate tenants using a custom header: `X-Tenant-ID`.

We'll rate limit the /metrics/memory endpoint. Each tenant should get 3 requests every 20 seconds.

Create an IdentityKeyResolver `TenantIdResolver.java`

```
package com.cloudmetrics.api;

import io.quarkiverse.bucket4j.runtime.resolver.IdentityResolver;

...

import jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped;
import jakarta.inject.Inject;

@ApplicationScoped
public class TenantIdResolver implements IdentityResolver {

    @Inject
    RoutingContext context;

    @Override
    public String getIdentityKey() {
        // Extract the tenant ID from the custom header
        String tenantId = context.request().getHeader("X-Tenant-ID");

        // If the header is not present, we can deny the request
        // or assign a default "anonymous" bucket. Here we deny.
        if (tenantId == null || tenantId.isBlank()) {
            // This will cause a 403 Forbidden because no key is resolved.
            return null;
        }
        return tenantId;
    }
}

...

Update the memory metrics endpoint:

```
@GET
@Path("/metrics/memory")
@RateLimited(bucket = "memory-metrics-limit", identityKey = TenantIdResolver.class)
public String getMemoryMetrics() {
    return "Memory usage: 58%";
}

...

And configure per-tenant limits:

```
# Per-tenant limit for the memory metrics endpoint
quarkus.rate-limiter.buckets.memory-metrics-limit.limits[0].permitted-uses=3
quarkus.rate-limiter.buckets.memory-metrics-limit.limits[0].period=20S
```

...

This time, we can’t just get away with convenient resolvers though. To achieve dynamic, tier-based rate limiting, we'll build a custom annotation and apply programmatic bucket resolution using the Bucket4j core API.

Create `@DynamicRateLimited` to mark endpoints with tier-aware throttling in `DynamicRateLimited.java:`

```
package com.cloudmetrics.api;

import jakarta.interceptor.InterceptorBinding;
import java.lang.annotation.*;

@InterceptorBinding
@Target({ ElementType.METHOD, ElementType.TYPE })
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface DynamicRateLimited {
}

...

return "Report generated for " + tenantContext.getTenantId();
    }
}

...

You just built a smart API gateway with Quarkus and Bucket4j that can:

- Enforce global throttling
- Limit by tenant ID

**Do a thin secure-by-default layer plus documentation — not a docs-only approach, and not a large security framework.**

The deciding rule: anything the library ships must be safe by default; operational choices can be documented.

### Do in code (small, high value)

1. **Fix shipped-code vulnerabilities** — unavoidable:
   - Java `FrameCodec` `opcodeCount` overflow/OOM + bounds checks.
   - TypeScript decoder caps, structural validation before applying a batch, and URL sanitization.

2. **Remove insecure defaults instead of documenting around them**:
   - Spring: stop hardcoding `setAllowedOrigins("*")`; add `pathland.allowed-origins` with same-origin default.
   - Quarkus: extension-contributed defaults for `quarkus.http.cors.enabled=true` (no `origins` = same-origin) and `quarkus.websockets-next.server.max-message-size`.

3. **Add default security headers in the existing SSR paths**:
   - A shared CSP/header constant in `server-core`.
   - Spring: set headers in `PathlandIndexController` (it already returns `ResponseEntity`).
   - Quarkus: same in `IndexResource`, or extension defaults via `quarkus.http.header.*`.
   - Override property, e.g. `pathland.content-security-policy`, so users can adjust.
   - This is roughly 30 lines total, not “a lot”.

4. **Add the per-session event rate breaker** in `PathlandSession`.
   - Edge rate limiting does not protect a single connected client from flooding the actor thread.
   - It is small and mirrors the existing proxy “chatty origin” breaker.

5. **SRI**: implement the small hash/manifest emission **or explicitly defer it**.
   - My recommendation: implement it, because #63 names it and it is cheap (manifest second line + `integrity` attribute).
   - If you want to minimize code, defer it with a documented rationale: same-origin, content-hashed bundle + `script-src 'self'` is already a strong posture.

### Document instead of code

Put these in `docs/SECURITY.md` or a README section, with copy-paste snippets for both hosts:

- TLS/WSS termination and trusted reverse-proxy headers.
- CSP rollout guidance (report-only first), and the reason `style-src 'unsafe-inline'` is required.

- Don’t write a custom CORS implementation for Quarkus; use its CORS filter.
- Don’t duplicate large Spring/Quarkus security filters; only wire secure defaults for the paths Pathland owns.
- Don’t document around the Spring wildcard or the decoder bugs — those are library defaults/bugs.

Need to decide on rate limiter implementation location and config. PathlandSession dispatch currently catches RuntimeException. Add fields:
```
private static final int MAX_BATCHES_PER_SECOND = Integer.getInteger("pathland.max-event-batches-per-second", 2000);
private long windowStart = System.nanoTime(); private int batchesInWindow;
private boolean allowEventBatch() { ... }
```
Per-session, called on actor thread, no sync needed. If false: LOG.warn + telemetry new method. Add telemetry method. Add config docs.

Alternatively rate limit at registry before enqueue to avoid actor queue flooding. Better: registry dispatch is called on event-loop thread; a per-session/connection counter in registry can drop before enqueue. But sessions are lazily created; registry has `uiId` key. Could maintain a `ConcurrentHashMap<String, Window>` in registry and remove on close. That protects actor queue, but adds map management. Simpler: in PathlandSession, the actor queue can still be flooded by 64K batches at high rate (each dispatch task). However decodeEvents happens on actor; so queue tasks are small references to byte[]. Flooding queue with many tasks consumes memory. Better to rate limit before enqueue in registry. But `PathlandSocket` calls `registry.dispatch` on the event loop; we can add a `PerConnectionRateLimiter` in registry keyed by sessionId. Or in the socket adapters themselves (per-connection state map) before calling registry. Quarkus endpoints already maintain `transports` map; could add counters there. But then duplicate in Spring. Better in registry: `ConcurrentHashMap<String, long[]>`? Since dispatch is called from multiple event-loop threads but per connection serialized? Not guaranteed; use synchronized/atomic per entry. A `ConcurrentHashMap<String, TokenBucket>` with `AtomicLong` windowStart/AtomicInteger count. Remove on close. That is small.

But note tests may dispatch many events in a tight loop (MultiSessionProbe 100 sessions each click) but per-session rate is low. Fine.

Could also cap total queued events/bytes per connection. Not necessary.

Now the "prioritize Quarkus" means:
- Quarkus extension gets secure defaults (CORS, headers, max message size) automatically.
- Spring gets minimal fixes: remove wildcard, add property. Maybe also add headers in controller? Since "prioritize" not "ignore", I'd still add headers to Spring controller because it's 5 lines and consistent. But plan says Spring parity for CSP is secondary; can be a follow-up. Let's decide: implement both because shared constant makes it trivial; but sequence Quarkus first. The user explicitly said prioritize Quarkus, so I'll say Spring gets only the mandatory wildcard fix + docs, with the shared CSP header optionally applied in the controller as a low-cost parity item (or defer). Hmm. To avoid scope creep and honor priority: 
  - Spring PR: fix wildcard (must), add property. Document CSP/header setup. SRI is shared PathlandSession so Spring gets it automatically. CSP could be added to Spring controller cheaply; I'd include it since it's the same helper and tests. But if prioritize means less Spring work, maybe don't add Spring-specific CSP filter. The controller approach is tiny. I'll include it as "optional/low-effort parity" and mark deferrable.
- Quarkus docs and config.

Now, one more important thing: SRI with Quarkus static resources. The SSR script tag is emitted by server-core; SRI works regardless of host. Good.

Now, Quarkus headers and CSP: if extension contributes `quarkus.http.header...` defaults, headers apply to all responses. But `Content-Security-Policy` on WebSocket upgrade responses? Harmless. On static JS? Ignored. Fine.

However, using `RunTimeConfigurationDefaultBuildItem` for headers might set CSP on the demo and break inline styles? We include `style-src 'unsafe-inline'`, so fine. But the demo may use data: images? We include `img-src 'self' data:`. Media from disk under `/_pathland/assets` self. Fine. The Quarkus demo has `pathland.demo.ad-url` proxy server-side, no browser. Good.

One issue: `connect-src 'self' ws: wss:` permits any ws host. Could construct policy with the actual host? The extension can't know it. Keep ws: wss:. Fine.

Now, documenting "how to secure in Spring Boot and Quarkus" — the deliverable should be a docs file. Since the user asked originally about docs vs code and chose include SRI, prioritize Quarkus. We should include docs in plan.

Now need to produce final plan, likely no further research needed. But maybe check if there are existing docs conventions (docs dir?). Let's list root.

# Pathland > An open UI protocol. Declarative UI — written once in any language, rendered natively anywhere. **Status: proof of concept.** It works end to end and the tests are green, but the wire format and APIs may change before 1.0. [![CI](https://github.com/PathlandDev/Pathland/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/PathlandDev/Pathland/actions/workflows/ci.yml) ## Pathland is a protocol Pathland is first and foremost a **binary UI protocol** — not just a framework, and not a single rendering target. Your view declaration compiles to fixed 16-byte opcodes that any renderer applies to native elements. The wire is the contract: a view written in Kotlin, Rust, or any other supported DSL produces the **same opcode stream**, and any renderer can apply it. That makes Pathland **language- and renderer-agnostic**: - **Write the UI once, declaratively.** A SwiftUI-shaped DSL in your language of choice — Kotlin, Rust, anything — describes the same view structure, whatever it later runs on. - **Run it on any surface.** The same view code drives today's server-rendered web and the native GTK4 desktop renderer, and is on track for the browser via WASM, embedded chips (LVGL), and native mobile/desktop (SwiftUI/UIKit, Jetpack Compose, Qt) ([Where it's headed](#where-its-headed)). - **Only changes travel.** The protocol is a stream of tiny binary deltas: an unchanged screen transmits zero bytes, and updates are applied in place. **Server-side rendering is the first surface we ship** — the flagship getting-started path — **not the whole story**. It's the on-ramp that's useful today; the protocol underneath is where the portability comes from. ## See it in action The same shared demo views, rendered by two of Pathland's surfaces — server-side HTML in the browser and native GTK4 widgets on the desktop:

Browser — SSR + live WebSocket deltas
Desktop — native GTK4 renderer
Try the hosted Quarkus demo live: **[pathland.onrender.com](https://pathland.onrender.com)**. ## The flagship path today: SSR The fastest way to replace a BFF + JavaScript-frontend stack. You write the **whole UI in your backend language** — Kotlin, Rust, anything. Pathland renders the first page as server-side HTML, so it appears instantly, then keeps it alive with tiny binary updates over a WebSocket. The result is a smooth, reactive UI — delivered by

# Security Policy

Pathland is a network-facing binary protocol: the byte decoders and the C ABI
are security-critical surfaces. This policy covers how vulnerabilities are
reported and handled.

## Reporting a vulnerability

**Do not open a public issue for a security vulnerability.** Report it privately
to the maintainers:

- Email: `michael@apaq.dk`
- Subject prefix: `[Pathland security]`

Please include:

- The affected crate/module and version (or commit).
- A description of the vulnerability and its impact.
- A minimal reproduction (payload bytes or code) where possible.
- Any suggested fix, if you have one.

We aim to acknowledge reports within **5 business days** and to ship a fix (or a
mitigation) as soon as a coordinated patch is ready. We will credit reporters in
the release notes unless anonymity is requested.

## Scope

The following are in scope for this policy:

- `lib/rust/crates/pathland-core` — the `no_std` protocol core (opcode decode,
  ring buffer, arena, memory layout).
- `lib/rust/crates/pathland-core-transport` — PLPL batch encode/decode.
- `lib/rust/crates/pathland-core-capi` — the `unsafe extern "C"` ring ABI
  (`libpathland_core`): pointer-argument handling, zero-copy reads, event drain.
- `lib/java/pathland-view-core` `transport` — `FrameCodec` (PLPL encode/decode).
- The `@pathland/dom-renderer` web client (PLPL batch decode + hydration in
  `lib/typescript/src`, built to `dist/pathland-dom-renderer.js` and copied into
  both demos).

Out of scope: dependencies (report those to their respective projects),
development-only tooling, and the demo application code.

## Security-sensitive guarantees

- Every 16-byte opcode decoder must **reject malformed/truncated input
  gracefully** (no panics, no out-of-bounds reads, no hangs) — see the hardening
  issues (#37, #38).
- The C ABI entry points (`pathland_ring_buffer_push`,
  `pathland_core_arena_alloc`, `pathland_core_drain_events`, …) treat
  caller-provided pointers as trusted by contract; the bounds guarantees must be
  upheld and are audited via Miri/sanitizers in CI.
- No secrets or tokens may ever be committed; see
  [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md).

## Security testing

Coverage is tracked by the hardening milestone (issues #37–#39): fuzzing for the
Rust/TypeScript/Java decoders, Miri + ASan/UBSan on the C ABI, and bounds fixes.
Results will be linked here as they land.

## Supported versions

The project is pre-1.0 (`wire protocol version 1`). Security fixes land on the
default branch and are backported only when a tagged release is actively used;
see the [Versioning](README.md#versioning) section.---DOCS---
